summary: A 1974 note on how the facilities used for TIP and TENEX accounting could be reused for collecting data from many sites across the network, beyond accounting alone. It explores the wider usefulness of those protocols.

eli5.summary: A tool made for counting who used the network could also gather other facts from many places. This note asks if it should.

subtitle: Protocol for collecting data reliably from multiple distributed servers

tldr.problem: Data collection in networks with multiple redundant servers risks either losing data or duplicating it. Systems need to reliably deliver data to exactly one server without losing or repeating data.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol uses a three-phase handshake: data generators broadcast to multiple servers, servers buffer and acknowledge, and the generator sends a final go-ahead to one server and discard messages to others, combined with sequence numbering to prevent duplicates.
tldr.outcome: The technique has wide applicability beyond the TIP accounting system for which it was developed, enabling reliable distributed data collection across networks.

facts.label: Retransmission interval
facts.value: 30 minutes normal, 5 minutes if server not responding

today: RFC 672 describes a protocol developed for TIP-TENEX accounting in 1974. The technique of three-phase distributed data collection has influenced later reliable delivery systems, though the specific protocol and systems described are now obsolete.

sections.title: The Problem of Reliable Distributed Data Collection
sections.content:
RFC 672 describes protocols for collecting data from multiple network sites to multiple data collection servers. The initial motivation was handling TIP accounting (tracking network usage) using TENEX systems as the collector servers.

The challenge is this: when you send data to multiple possible servers for redundancy, you avoid losing data if one server fails. But you risk duplicating data if multiple servers all process the same request. If you wait for an acknowledgment and it times out, should you resend to another server or the same one? Different choices have different consequences.
sections.eli5: When data goes to multiple computers for safety, you need a way to make sure it ends up saved exactly once, not lost or saved twice.

sections.title: The Three-Phase Protocol
sections.content:
The data collector uses a three-phase approach. First, the data source (a TIP) sends its data to some or all accounting servers. Each server that receives the message buffers it and sends back an acknowledgment saying "I've got it". Second, the source examines the replies and picks one server to get the data: it sends a "go ahead" message to that server. Third, it sends a "discard" message to all other servers that acknowledged.

To prevent duplicate data even when messages are retransmitted, the TIP includes a sequence number with each data message. If an old delayed acknowledgment arrives after the TIP has moved to a new sequence number, it will be rejected as obsolete.
sections.eli5: The data generator offers to many servers, picks the one that responds first, tells that one to keep it, and tells the others to throw it away.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content:
In the initial TIP-TENEX implementation, the TIP sends accounting data about once every half hour. If no server acknowledges within the timeout, the TIP speeds up to trying every 5 minutes until it succeeds. The TIP maintains a "favored" server—the one that most recently accepted data—and tries that one first. If it does not respond, the TIP broadcasts to all servers and accepts whichever replies first.

The 16-bit sequence number field is large enough that even if a host crashes and restarts, the probability of sequence number confusion is negligible. The protocol is robust against lost or garbled transmissions, since retransmission is the normal procedure.
sections.eli5: The TIP remembers which server usually works best and tries it first. If it does not answer, the TIP asks all servers and picks the fastest one.

sections.title: Applicability Beyond Accounting
sections.content: The protocol is designed for data that is either independent (like recording names) or follows a commutative relationship (like counting). This allows retransmitting different versions of the data to different servers without losing coherence. The technique can be adapted for other distributed data collection problems that require either avoiding duplicates or avoiding losses, depending on the application's priorities.
sections.eli5: The technique works for many kinds of data collection, not just counting network use. Different applications can adapt it depending on whether they fear losing data more or duplicating it.
